extracted.intended_audience: computer scientists, software-verification engineers, and students learning to use the Coq proof assistant
extracted.subtask_description: A tutorial introducing the Coq proof assistant and its use for practical software verification: core architecture, basic commands and tactics, inductive definitions, libraries, proof automation (including reflection), and guidelines for verifying programs and using libraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trusted kernel architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq is based on a two levels architecture: a relatively small kernel with few primitive constructions and rules for type-checking and computation, and a richer user environment on top of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because proofs and definitions are ultimately checked by the small trusted kernel, one may extend the environment (notations, tactics, libraries) safely: "This environment can be used and extended safely because ultimately any definition and proof is checked by a safe kernel." Example: the kernel checks the term extracted from tactics at Qed/Save.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof safety: avoid leftover axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Safety in Coq is only guaranteed if there are no axioms left in the proof development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using admit or finishing proofs with Admitted introduces axioms and is potentially dangerous: "Assuming a false property might result in being able to prove ⊥ and, consequently, everything becomes provable." Use Print Assumptions name to list axioms used. Anti-pattern: leaving proofs Admitted in a development intended to be trusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to verify programs with Coq
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq can be used for program verification in multiple ways (each with trade-offs): (1) express program correctness as a mathematical statement and prove it; (2) implement an analyzer in Coq and prove the analyzer correct; (3) represent program as a Coq term whose type encodes the specification (t : T); (4) use an external tool to generate proof obligations and solve them in Coq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-offs: method (1) guarantees correctness but can be hard; (2) is a huge investment but yields automatic guaranteed results; (3) works well for functional or monadic programs; (4) is less safe unless the generator is certified but can handle undecidable fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inductive definitions for data and relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive definitions capture data-types, logical connectives and primitive relations; they introduce constructors and automatically generate induction principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Syntax: Inductive name : sort := c1 : C1 | ... | cn : Cn. Inductive types must obey syntactic restrictions to ensure well-foundedness. Examples: bool, nat, prod; the declaration generates lemmas like nat_ind. Use inductive Prop to define logical connectives (e.g., or, False) so their proofs carry computational content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern-matching and exhaustive cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Define functions and case-analysis with match ... with; patterns are examined sequentially and must cover the whole domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalized pattern-matching compiles to primitive patterns. Example: match n, m with | O, _ => false | _, O => false | _, _ => true end. Anti-pattern: leaving non-exhaustive matches; be aware generalized matches are compiled away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Sections, Variables, Hypotheses to structure context
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Section name, Variable(s) and Hypothesis to introduce local contexts shared by several definitions; End abstracts definitions over those variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lets you write definitions depending on local parameters and then automatically obtain polymorphic versions after ending the section. Example: Section test. Variable A : Type. Variables x y : A. Definition double : A * A := (x,x). End test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library and namespace management
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage modules and libraries with Require Import, Require, Print Libraries, Print LoadPath, Locate, SearchAbout, About and Qualifed names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require Import name loads and opens modules; Require name loads but keeps qualified names; SearchAbout and SearchAbout [names] help find lemmas mentioning identifiers or patterns. Use Print Libraries and Print LoadPath to inspect available modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer existing standard libraries for domains (numbers, floats, machine integers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Coq's standard or external libraries for arithmetic, machine integers and floating point (e.g., ZArith, Int31, CompCert Integers, Reals, Flocq) rather than re-implementing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ZArith provides Z and Zabs; CompCert/Int library for machine integers; Flocq for IEEE floating-point. Be aware of modeling differences (e.g., machine integers modulo 2^N) and the need to Open Scope (Z_scope, R_scope) to use usual notations. Anti-pattern: mixing representations without care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactic-based backward reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tactics to perform backward reasoning: a tactic turns a goal into subgoals until none remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary tactics: intros (multiple introductions), apply (use a lemma), destruct (case analysis), assert (forward reasoning). Use tacticals: t1; t2 (apply t2 to subgoals), t1 || t2, try t, repeat t. Examples and the correspondence with natural deduction rules are given in the tutorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automation tactics judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq provides automation tactics (auto, trivial, tauto, intuition, omega, contradiction) that perform proof search for common patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: auto searches a lemma database; tauto solves propositional tautologies; omega solves linear arithmetic; contradiction detects False or A and ¬A. Use these to discharge routine subgoals but be aware limits (e.g., automation on reals is limited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality handling tactics and rewrite strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use equality tactics (rewrite, rewrite <-, replace, subst, symmetry, transitivity, f_equal) to manipulate equalities and perform substitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: rewrite by default replaces all occurrences; rewrite H at occs rewrites selected occurrences. replace u with t generates a subgoal u = t. subst substitutes variables when x = t occurs with x not in t. Use reflexivity for convertible terms. Example: rewrite H to apply an equality hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof finishing and kernel check (Qed/Save)
rubrics_metrics.description: After building a proof with tactics, Coq extracts a proof term and the trusted kernel checks Γ ⊢ p : A at Qed or Save.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extra checking allows freely extending tactics without compromising safety. Use Qed to finalize and record theorem; be aware some checks (universes, termination) happen only at end and rare cases may lead to incorrect finished proof if those checks fail earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Print Assumptions to audit dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Print Assumptions name displays all axioms and assumptions used in theorem name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to ensure that a theorem does not depend on unexpected axioms (e.g., excluded middle) and to verify trustworthiness of a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with admit/Admitted
rubrics_metrics.description: admit introduces an axiom for the current goal and Admitted records the theorem as an axiom; these undermine soundness if left in final developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit/Admitted are useful for prototyping but dangerous for trusted developments. Anti-pattern: shipping developments with Admitted theorems when reliability is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical vs intuitionistic logic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq implements intuitionistic logic by default (A ∨ ¬A is not an axiom); classical reasoning requires adding the excluded middle or importing Classical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many constructions are constructive and allow computation from proofs (e.g., ∃ and ∨ carry witnesses). If classical logic is needed, import a library like Classical but be aware it adds axioms; prefer constructive proofs when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-by-reflection (reification) for automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection reduces proving propositions to computation by reifying propositions into data, computing a boolean decision procedure, and checking that the computation yields true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: (1) implement a reification mapping from propositions to closed terms p; (2) implement r2b and prove its correctness; (3) ensure r2b p reduces efficiently to true. Reflection is used in tactics like ring, omega, setoid rewrite and for building certified decision procedures. Trade-offs: p should be small and closed to compute; r2b must be efficient and proven correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Ltac for meta-programming and reification
rubrics_metrics.description: Ltac can be used to compute an environment and a reified formula from a goal, and to apply change to replace the goal by its reified interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the paper shows Ltac env_form and reify to turn 0=0 /	ing into a form and environment and then change the goal to f2P e f. Use Ltac to automate pattern-matching and reification steps carefully to avoid duplication (share subterms when possible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interfaces and editors effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graphical/textual interfaces like coqide or Emacs+ProofGeneral to interact with Coq; these provide windows for commands, goals, and queries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: coqide includes a Queries window and displays unsolved goals; ProofGeneral offers similar functionality. Recommendation: follow examples while experimenting in an interactive environment rather than reading only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Notation and implicit arguments for readable code
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Notation, Set Implicit Arguments and Implicit Arguments to make Coq code more concise and readable by letting Coq infer type arguments and provide convenient syntax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: declare Notation "[ x | y | z ]" for Triple x y z and Set Implicit Arguments to omit explicit type parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a proof assistant based on required features and libraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Select Coq or another assistant depending on needs: intuitionistic vs classical logic, need for dependent types, trust base and available libraries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical reasons often drive choice (team use, local expertise, existing libraries). The tutorial notes there is no single right choice; compare requirements (dependent types, libraries) before committing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate external provers via certified traces when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Many automated provers produce traces that can be checked inside Coq—use those traces or certified interfaces rather than trusting external tools unconditionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: SAT/SMT solvers producing traces that are then checked by Coq, termination tools integrated via certified witnesses. Why3 platform can translate problems to various provers and produce artifacts suitable for checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use computation to discharge trivial proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: When proof reduces to a computation on closed terms (e.g., booleans), finishing the proof can be done by computing and using reflexivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: computing r2b p ≡ true yields a trivial proof via computation (refl_eq). Use compute, simpl, and reflexivity for such cases; ensure terms are closed for full computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and reuse invariants for finite-state decision procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite but large state spaces (like the board example), design invariants and use reflection to build decision procedures that decide ∀b : board, P(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the board has a finite number of states, one can implement a reflective tactic that decides the property by computing invariants and verifying reachability. Use reification and decision procedures tailored to the finite domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about scopes when using different numeric notations
rubrics_metrics.description: Open the appropriate scope (e.g., Z_scope, R_scope) to have usual arithmetic notations interpreted for the intended numeric type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after Require Import ZArith, use Open Scope Z_scope to make 0 and + denote integers rather than nat. This avoids confusing notation interpretation between nat, Z, R, etc.
